steps.body: To place **1/b** on the line: cut the 0→1 trip into b equal jumps, take ONE jump from 0, and land. That landing spot IS 1/b. The fraction names a spot — a distance from 0 — not a mark number.

widget.prompt: The 0→1 trip has 4 equal jumps. Slide the marker to the spot ONE jump from 0 — that's 1/4.
widget.lowFeedback: You're still at the trailhead — take the jump.
widget.highFeedback: Too far along — 1/4 is just ONE jump from 0. Slide back.
widget.successFeedback: One jump of the four: you're standing on 1/4, a quarter of the way to 1.

predict.prompt: You'll slide to 1/4 of the trip. Will that spot be nearer the START (0) or nearer the END (1)?
predict.reveal: One jump out of four barely leaves the trailhead — 1/4 sits close to 0, not near the 4th tick at the end.

explanationVariants: 1/6 is one jump of a six-jump trip — the FIRST mark after 0.
Read it as directions: cut into 6, take one jump. You've barely left home.

widget.prompt: On a 0→1 line split into 6 equal jumps, place the marker at 1/6.

commonPlacements.feedback: The sixth mark is six jumps — 6/6, which is 1, the whole trip. 1/6 is a single jump from 0.

widget.successFeedback: One jump in — the first landing of the trip.
widget.lowFeedback: Jumps run FORWARD from 0 — 1/6 sits a little way into the trip, not behind the start.
widget.highFeedback: Too far along — the 6 in 1/6 counts the JUMPS between 0 and 1; the TOP number says how many of them to take.

steps.body: Time to bust the big trap: **"1/4 sits at the 4-mark."** Backwards! The 4 in 1/4 is the CUT — it sets the jump size. The landing is always after ONE jump. The bottom number tells you how the trip was sliced, never where you stop.

explanationVariants: The fifth mark is five jumps: 5/5 — the complete trip, which is 1. 1/5 was back at the first mark.
Mark number = jump count = the TOP of the fraction. Five jumps of fifths make the whole.

widget.prompt: Nia placed 1/5 at the FIFTH mark and got it wrong. Place 1/5 where it really belongs.

commonPlacements.feedback: Five jumps of a five-cut trip: 5/5 = 1. Nia stood at the finish line, not at 1/5.

widget.successFeedback: The first mark — 1/5 is one jump from 0. (The fifth mark is 5/5 = 1, where Nia went wrong.)
widget.lowFeedback: 0 is the start, before any jumps.
widget.highFeedback: Too many jumps — each mark is one more fifth. Count how many jumps 1/5 needs.

steps.body: Match each unit to its landing.

widget.prompt: Connect each unit fraction to where it lands on the 0→1 trip.

right.label: One tiny jump from 0, of eight

pairErrors.feedback: Halfway would be 4/8 — four of the eight tiny jumps. A single eighth-jump barely leaves 0.

widget.missFeedback: Every unit fraction is ONE jump from 0 — the bottom number only sets how big that jump is.
widget.successFeedback: 1/2 lands halfway, 1/3 at the first of three marks, 1/8 a tiny hop from 0 — one jump each, different jump sizes.

explanationVariants: An eight-cut makes tiny jumps — one of them barely leaves 0. A three-cut's single jump is a big stride.
More jumps in the same trip means each jump is shorter — so 1/8 lands nearer to 0 than 1/3.

widget.prompt: Which spot is CLOSER to 0: 1/8 or 1/3?

options.feedback: Eight tiny jumps share the trip — one of them is a short hop, landing close to 0.
The big-number reflex on the line! An 8-cut makes SMALLER jumps than a 3-cut — so 1/8 lands nearer 0, not farther.

options.label: They share a spot
options.feedback: Different cuts, different jump sizes, different landings — 1/8 sits well short of 1/3.

options.label: Impossible to tell
options.feedback: The line tells all: one eighth-jump is shorter than one third-jump, so 1/8 stays closer to home.

hints: The bottom of 1/7 records how the trip was cut.
The first mark is exactly one jump from 0.
If one jump is 1/7 of the trip, how many jumps finish it?
explanationVariants: 1/7 at the first mark means each jump is a seventh of the trip — so the whole trip takes 7 jumps.
The bottom number IS the jump count of the full trip: sevenths → seven jumps to reach 1.

widget.prompt: On a 0→1 line cut into equal jumps, the FIRST mark is exactly 1/7. How many jumps does the whole trip have?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is how many jumps reach the first mark. The question asks about the WHOLE trip — and its jumps are sevenths, so it takes 7.
6 counts the INSIDE marks (jumps − 1). The trip itself has one more jump than inside marks: 7.

widget.fallbackFeedback: One jump covers 1/7 of the trip — count how many sevenths make the whole.

steps.body: You can land any unit now.
takeaways: 1/b = one jump from 0 on a b-jump trip.
The bottom number sets the jump SIZE — it is never the landing mark.
Bigger bottoms make shorter jumps: 1/8 lands closer to 0 than 1/3.
steps.teaser: next: stacking jumps to land a/b — counting your way up the line.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Read 1/b as walking directions: **"cut the trip into b jumps; take one."** 1/4? Cut into four, take one jump — you're standing on 1/4, with three jumps still ahead.

explanationVariants: One jump of a four-jump trip lands on the first mark — that's 1/4.
Directions: cut into 4, take one. First mark, every time.

widget.prompt: On a 4-jump line from 0 to 1, where is 1/4?

options.label: The first mark after 0
options.feedback: One jump in — that's the spot.

options.label: The fourth mark
options.feedback: Four jumps is 4/4 = 1, the far end. One jump lands 1/4.

options.label: At the number 4
options.feedback: The 4 sets the jump size — it isn't a destination. 1/4 is one jump from 0.
